blk_part_02_part_2_between_sweden_and_ru.text: Swedish rule ended after the Finnish War of 1808–1809. Finland then became an autonomous Grand Duchy within the Russian Empire. It kept many Swedish laws, while Helsinki became the capital in 1812. Finnish national culture also grew: Elias Lönnrot published the Kalevala in 1835, and an 1863 language decree began raising Finnish toward official status. In 1906, Finland created a one-chamber parliament and became the first European country to give women both the vote and the right to stand for election.

blk_part_03_part_3_independence_and_a_di.text: However, the new country quickly divided. From January to May 1918, the socialist Reds fought the government-supported Whites. The Whites won with help from German troops. The Battle of Tampere was the bloodiest battle, and prison camps caused many later deaths from hunger and disease. Altogether, about 38,000 people died in a population of roughly three million. The conflict left deep political and social wounds. Nevertheless, Finland adopted a republican constitution in 1919, and Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg became its first president.

A major Soviet offensive captured Viipuri in June 1944, but Finnish forces stopped further advances at battles including Tali-Ihantala. Across the two Soviet wars, Finland lost about 12 percent of its land, but it was not occupied and its democratic state survived.
